questions.prompt: "Put it in the bin" is the first sentence of a session. What should the parser do?
options: Choose the last object mentioned by the robot.
Return a goal with the nearest object.
Return Clarify asking which object is meant.
Return Unparseable and stay silent about why.
questions.explanation: A pronoun without an antecedent is an ambiguity, so ask.

questions.prompt: Why is "zero wrong-but-confident parses on adversarial sentences" a hard zero rather than a percentage?
options: A wrong parse leads to a wrong physical action.
Adversarial sentences are too rare to compute a percentage.
The parser is judged on the exact-match rate only.
Percentages cannot be computed on ten sentences.
questions.explanation: Refusing is cheap; executing the wrong action is not.

questions.prompt: Design five adversarial sentences for the tidy-up parser and state what each must return and why.
rubric: Covers at least four different failure types (unsafe verb, negation, unknown colour, too many objects, pronoun, contradiction with the scene).
States Clarify or Unparseable for each with a reason.
Explains that none may return a goal.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Robot starts away from the table, goal is one object into a bin. Minimum number of actions (nav, pick, nav, place)?
Why does the planner have an expansion cap even though breadth-first search with a visited set terminates?
options: To make the plan longer so it is safer.
To bound the time on unreachable problems and return None.
Because breadth-first search can loop forever on repeated states.
To make the plan optimal.
questions.explanation: Termination is not the same as bounded time; the cap protects real-time behaviour.

questions.prompt: Start at the table, two objects into the same bin, one gripper. Minimum number of actions?
questions.explanation: pick, nav, place, nav, pick, nav, place = 7.

questions.prompt: A pick succeeds with probability 0.7 per try, independently, with at most two retries. Probability the pick eventually succeeds (3 decimals).
Why limit retries to two and then abort or replan with a reason?
options: Because a third try always succeeds.
Because behaviour trees cannot repeat children more than twice.
Repeated failures usually share a cause, so extra retries waste time and hide the real fault.
Because retries make the robot move faster.
questions.explanation: Attempts are rarely independent; the abort reason is what the planner or the user needs.

questions.prompt: What does a tick bound in the behaviour tree runner protect against?
options: A skill that is too accurate.
Memory leaks in the parser.
Serial frames with a bad checksum.
A bug or a never-finishing node hanging the whole task.
questions.explanation: Every loop in the task layer needs a bound that is tested.

questions.prompt: Human-zone speed 0.15 m/s, reaction time 0.3 s, deceleration 1 m/s squared. Stopping distance in metres (3 decimals).
questions.skillLabel: Safety time budget and stopping distance

questions.prompt: Heartbeat timeout is 0.2 s and the supervisor tick is 10 ms. Margin in milliseconds to the 300 ms requirement.
questions.skillLabel: Safety time budget and stopping distance

questions.prompt: In 20 nominal episodes the supervisor stopped the robot in 6 of them with no injected hazard. What is the most useful reaction?
options: Accept it, because stopping is always the safe thing to do.
Log the reasons, raise the thresholds that fired above nominal and recheck the injection times.
Disable the supervisor during all nominal runs from now on.
Remove the hazards that fired from the hazard table.
questions.explanation: Nuisance stops are a defect; fix them with data without breaking the time budget.

questions.prompt: Write the paragraph of docs/safety_architecture.md that explains why the supervisor is independent of the planner and what it does not protect against.
rubric: Names the mechanisms of independence: own process or thread and clock, sensor and heartbeat inputs, direct firmware stop.
Lists at least two things it does not protect against (for example a wrong camera image, a bug in the supervisor itself).
States clearly that it protects a simulation and is not certified safety.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Design the injection test for "serial link dead for 200 ms": inputs, how you measure time to the safe state, the pass limit and one boundary case.
rubric: Describes injecting link age growing from the injection time, with nominal inputs otherwise.
Measures the time from injection to forwarded velocity zero and arm hold, at the 10 ms tick.
Gives the limit (300 ms) and a boundary case such as a link age just below the timeout that must not trigger.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
